source: Cook, Goodman & Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Exp 1: preschoolers who saw ambiguous evidence (only some bead pairs work) pulled apart the separable pair and tested each bead. Those who saw unambiguous evidence (all beads work) almost never did.
numbers: N=60 (3 conditions of 20). Informative experiment: All Beads 1/20 (5%), Some Beads B 9/20 (45%), Some Beads AB 10/20 (50%). Chi2(1,N=40)=8.53 and 10.16, both p<.005. 65% of All Beads children never pulled the pair apart.
limits: Four toy objects, two bead pairs, one machine. Strict coding: each bead had to be tested separately. Intercoder agreement 95% (kappa .90).
agent_relevance: Action value depends on whether the evidence is ambiguous. Code should compute that gap, not assume every test is worth running.

source: Cook, Goodman & Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Exp 2: with a stuck bead pair, children given ambiguous evidence invented a new action, standing the pair vertically so each end could be tested alone. Unambiguous-evidence children almost never did.
numbers: N=40. All Beads 1/20 (5%) vs Some Beads 9/20 (45%) performed the informative intervention. Chi2(1,N=40)=8.53, p<.005. Hypothesis-blind coder agreement 86% (kappa .71).
limits: The action was not in the usual play repertoire, so this is generation of a test, not just choice among known tests. More than half the ambiguous group still did not do it.
agent_relevance: Candidate-test generation is a separate step from scoring. A scaffold needs a step that invents discriminating tests, then scores them.

source: Cook, Goodman & Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Control: ambiguity did not simply make children play more or more widely. Number of play categories was the same across conditions.
numbers: Mean play categories about 3.8 in Exp 1 (no difference across conditions); about 3.0 in Exp 2 Some Beads, t(40)=0.89, ns. Other (non-target) actions: no Fisher exact comparison significant.
limits: This rules out the rival account that more variable play just stumbles on the test. Authors still note that random variety would help even without sensitivity.
agent_relevance: When comparing a smart explorer with a random one, count breadth of actions as a control. Gains should come from selection, not volume.

source: Cook, Goodman & Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Authors state the model: EIG of an action A depends on the prior over hypotheses P(H) and on action affordances P(D|A,H). Children appear to combine both.
numbers: Formal: EIG(A) = prior entropy minus expected posterior entropy. No sample-size number beyond Exp 1 N=60 and Exp 2 N=40.
quote: This study does not establish however, whether children understood the importance of isolating variables
limits: The paper does not fit a computed EIG to individual children. It is a qualitative match to the model. Authors say it does not show children understood why isolating variables works.
agent_relevance: The match is to the direction of EIG, not to exact values. Do not claim children compute EIG.

source: Cook, Goodman & Schulz (2011) Where science starts: spontaneous experiments in preschoolers' exploratory play
finding: Boundary conditions in the discussion: simple toy world with two to four variables, tight control of what is presented, one-session play.
numbers: Mean age about 54 months. Exp 1 exclusions: 6 for experimental error. Exp 2 exclusions: 5 (experimental error, parental interference, refusal).
limits: Authors say real life is less clear-cut and call for ecologically valid tests. Play serves other goals too (sensorimotor, skill).
agent_relevance: Do not assume the human result generalises to open-ended tasks. The agent should enforce the information check in code where humans do it only in toy settings.

source: Hu, Liu, Feng et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: uncertainty-aware planning enhances information seeking in LLMs
finding: UoT simulates possible answers, scores each question by information gain over the remaining possibilities, and picks the best by reward propagation. It beats direct prompting on 20 Questions, medical diagnosis and troubleshooting.
numbers: Average success-rate gain 38.1% over direct prompting across LLMs and 5 datasets. Llama3-70B gain 46.6%. UoT beats CoT-SC by 33.8%, Reflexion by 29.9%, original ToT by 28.3%, adapted ToT by 12.4%. Troubleshooting GPT-4: 43.7% to 67.3%. MedDG UoT (closed set) 81.4% (Gemini-1.5-Pro), 88.0% (GPT-4).
limits: Answerer is simulated by GPT-4 (checked on 10% of dialogues). Closed-set tasks are easier. Gains are average success-rate, not paired significance tests. Answers like 'no fever' do not fully rule out cases.
agent_relevance: Direct match to the idea: compute information gain over an explicit candidate set. Large measured gains with GPT-4-class models.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts, ablation
finding: Ablation: adding the uncertainty-based reward to a plain tree-of-thought search raises success. UoT still beats the tree-of-thought variant that uses a model self-evaluation reward.
numbers: Adding the uncertainty reward to Adapted-ToT raised efficacy by 5.9% on average. UoT beats Adapted-ToT by 12.4%. Pruned UoT beats Adapted-ToT by 7.36% at lower cost.
limits: Search depth and pruning interact with the reward; compute is higher than direct prompting.
agent_relevance: The information-gain reward itself, not just search, carries part of the gain. Keep scoring in code, not in the model's self-rating.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts, 20 Questions
finding: On 20 Questions, chain-of-thought and plan-and-solve (closed set) do worse than plain GPT-4. UoT is best.
numbers: UoT (open set) averages 8.7% above the other tested methods on GPT-4 and 4.3% above Reflexion, the second best. CoT (CS) and PP (CS) fall below GPT-4 direct.
limits: Closed-set (CS) vs open-set (OS) variants differ. Exact per-model numbers are in Table 5 of the paper and were not all extracted.
agent_relevance: More thinking text does not make a model ask better questions. Explicit partition-scoring does.

source: Kobalczyk, Astorga, Liu & van der Schaar (2025) Active task disambiguation with LLMs (ICLR 2025)
finding: Frames clarifying questions as Bayesian experimental design. Sample candidate solutions, have the model answer each candidate question for each sample, and pick the question whose answers split the samples most evenly (EIG-uniform). This beats asking the model to reason in question space.
numbers: On 20 Questions with GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4o-mini, EIG-uniform outperforms implicit, implicit-ToT and EIG-logprobs by a significant margin (15 animals, 5 run seeds, 25 evaluation seeds). N=20 sampled solutions gave a good proxy for the EIG on a 500-animal list. Fewer compatible animals remain after each round.
quote: shifts the load from implicit to explicit reasoning about the space of viable solutions
limits: Gap to implicit methods is much smaller for the stronger GPT-4o-mini. Exact effect sizes are given only as plotted curves.
agent_relevance: Reason in solution space, not question space. Estimating EIG with sampled hypotheses is cheap and a code step.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025) Active task disambiguation, code tasks
finding: The same EIG selection is tested on clarifying questions for code with a cap of 4 questions on competition-level coding problems.
numbers: Four-question budget; accuracy by iteration is plotted. Exact table values were not extracted in this session.
limits: Estimation depends on diverse solution samples; the paper has a study on solution diversity. LLM hallucination of requirements rises as constraints pile up.
agent_relevance: Sample diversity is a boundary condition: if hypotheses are all alike, EIG is near zero and misleading.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025) Active task disambiguation, theory
finding: Max EIG of a question is at most log of the number of hypotheses. For binary questions, the best question splits the hypotheses into two equal halves. Questions with many answer options give more bits but cost more effort for the user.
numbers: EIG(q) = H[p(h|S)] - E_a H[p(h|S plus (q,a))]; bound log|H|. Utility U(q)=EIG(q) - c(q).
limits: The cost term c(q) is hand-set; the paper notes that humans may answer wrongly and that p(a|q) may violate truthfulness.
agent_relevance: Add a cost term to the information score. A pure EIG maximiser asks long compound questions.

source: Kobalczyk et al. (2025), failure of log-probability EIG
finding: Using the LLM's own token probabilities to weight candidate solutions (EIG-logprobs) did worse than uniform weights over sampled solutions.
numbers: EIG-logprobs significantly below EIG-uniform on 20 Questions for GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4o-mini.
limits: The explanation given is that the model's distribution favours solutions that do not agree with the true candidate set.
agent_relevance: Do not trust the model's own probabilities as the prior. Use explicit, uniform or evidence-based weights.

source: Mazzaccara, Testoni & Bernardi (2024) Learning to ask informative questions: preference optimisation and expected information gain
finding: Training Llama-2-Chat 7B with DPO on pairs of high-EIG vs low-EIG questions from 20 Questions raises question informativeness and success. Plain supervised fine-tuning on high-EIG questions lowers success.
numbers: Test sets with 8 candidates: INLG success@1 zero-shot 56.7%, fine-tune 46.6%, DPO 68.9%; mean EIG 0.34, 0.41, 0.45. Things: 51.1%, 42.2%, 61.1%; EIG 0.29, 0.31, 0.40. Celebrities: 71.1%, 46.7%, 72.2%; EIG 0.35, 0.39, 0.47. Training pairs: 55,000 (EIG=1 vs EIG<0.8).
limits: Fine-tuning raised EIG yet lowered success. Out of domain (BigBench), EIG slightly fell, 0.31 to 0.28. Gains fall with larger candidate sets.
agent_relevance: Higher EIG per question did not always give higher success. Use code-scored EIG as a filter signal, not the whole objective.

source: Mazzaccara et al. (2024), zero-shot baseline
finding: Zero-shot LLM questions are far below optimal. An optimal 20 Questions question splits items into two equal-size clusters; open-source LLMs seldom do this.
numbers: Zero-shot mean EIG 0.29 to 0.35 on a 0 to 1 scale across test sets, with 7.1 to 7.6 questions per game. DPO cut questions to about 5.1 to 5.2.
limits: Scale is per-question EIG normalised so 1 is a perfect half split. Only a 7B open model was trained.
agent_relevance: Out of the box a model gets about a third of the possible information per question. Computing the split in code can close the gap.

source: Bertolazzi et al. (2023) ChatGPT's information seeking strategy, as cited by Mazzaccara et al.
finding: Mazzaccara et al. report that earlier work found LLMs play 20 Questions with low informativeness and limited success.
numbers: No figures read from the original Bertolazzi paper in this session.
limits: Secondhand, from related-work text; the original paper was not opened.
agent_relevance: Treat as a pointer; verify before citing numbers.

source: Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le & Ellis (2024) Doing experiments and revising rules with natural language and probabilistic reasoning
finding: An LLM proposes natural-language rules, sequential Monte Carlo weights them against data, and experiments are chosen by information gain. Human-model comparison on Zendo; the online (experiment-by-experiment) method beats batch methods at finding the rule.
numbers: Zendo predictive accuracy (5 seeds): human 5.26; direct LLM (ReAct) 4.60; batch fuzzy 5.35; online fuzzy 6.01. Other hard-rule rows are 6.18 and 6.55 in the garbled table. ActiveACRE task solving: batch hard 0.15, online hard 0.35, fuzzy variants 0.00.
limits: Table extraction was noisy, so row-to-number mapping needs a check. Fuzzy (probabilistic) rules fit humans better; hard rules score higher but fit humans worse.
agent_relevance: Information-gain experiment choice on top of an LLM hypothesis proposer outperformed humans. A human-like fit needed noisy beliefs, so max-EIG is a ceiling, not a person model.

source: Piriyakulkij et al. (2024), human fit
finding: Which model explains human Zendo behaviour best: the online fuzzy-rule model. A direct LLM player correlates poorly with human accuracy per rule.
numbers: Online fuzzy model explains 57% of variance in per-rule human accuracy. Direct LLM (ReAct) R2=.25. One batch variant R2=.05. Human data from Bramley et al.
limits: Tested on Zendo (10 rules) and one ACRE variant; not on open-ended science.
agent_relevance: LLMs alone do not pick informative experiments well; with an explicit belief state they do.

source: Piriyakulkij et al. (2024), random baseline
finding: Authors state that prior LLM methods for generating and revising hypotheses do not consistently beat random guessing when proposing experiments.
numbers: Qualitative statement in the introduction; specific comparison figures are in the experiments section.
quote: do not consistently outperform random guessing when proposing experiments
limits: The claim concerns the cited prior methods, not all LLM agents.
agent_relevance: A random-experiment baseline should be in every test of the agent's information step.

source: Grand, Pepe, Andreas & Tenenbaum (2024) Loose LIPS sink ships: asking questions in Battleship with language-informed program sampling (CogSci)
finding: Sample questions from an LLM, translate each to a program, score by EIG on the board, keep the best. A small sampling budget matches average human question quality. GPT-4 alone does not use the board well, and adding vision does not help.
numbers: Human data N=40, 605 board-question pairs, 18 boards. Mean human EIG 1.27 bits; best human question 3.61; 97% of human questions had EIG>0. One-sample CodeLlama-7b and GPT-4 questions: mean EIG 0.65 to 0.66. With more samples k the LIPS models reach the human mean; none reaches the best human question.
limits: Single-turn task in one game. Few-shot examples raised EIG; GPT-4V gained nothing from the image over text. Cost grows with k.
agent_relevance: Sample-then-score about doubles the EIG of one-shot generation. Generate many candidate tests, compute EIG in code, take the argmax.

source: Rothe, Lake & Gureckis (2017) Battleship questions, as used in Grand et al. (2024)
finding: Humans asked Battleship questions with no example prompts; question asking was modelled as program synthesis scored by EIG.
numbers: As reported in Grand et al.: 26 to 39 questions per board from 40 participants.
limits: Secondhand; original paper not opened.
agent_relevance: A human benchmark for question informativeness exists and can be reused.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023) Using cognitive psychology to understand GPT-3 (PNAS)
finding: On information-search vignettes GPT-3 chose the better question type in both Toma scenarios, copied the human congruence bias in a test-choice task, and gave the logically correct Wason answer (A and 7) where most people choose A and 4.
numbers: Toma: right question in both scenarios. Baron test choice: same wrong choice as people. Wason: A and 7. CRT: all 3 items intuitive wrong. 12 vignettes: 6 answered correctly, all 12 correct or human-like.
limits: Vignettes were probably in training data. Small changes to a vignette change the answer. One model (GPT-3 text-davinci era).
agent_relevance: Familiar textbook cases are not evidence that the model computes information value on novel problems.

source: Binz & Schulz (2023), bandit and causal tasks
finding: GPT-3 shows no sign of directed exploration (exploring to gain information) in a bandit task, though it beats humans on regret. It also fails the Blicket causal task.
numbers: Abstract: outperforms humans in a multi-armed bandit task, shows no signatures of directed exploration, fails miserably in causal reasoning (Blicket).
quote: it shows no signatures of directed exploration, and that it fails miserably in causal reasoning task
limits: Done with GPT-3 (2022); newer models not tested here.
agent_relevance: Good reward-chasing can hide missing information-seeking. Test the information step on its own.

source: Li, Tamkin, Goodman & Andreas (2023) Eliciting human preferences with language models (GATE)
finding: Letting the LM ask open-ended questions or write edge cases (generative active task elicitation) gave answers often more informative than user-written prompts or labelled examples, and users reported less effort.
numbers: Pre-registered, 3 domains (email validation, content recommendation, moral reasoning), 388 participants (Prolific plus students). Pool-based active learning was a baseline.
limits: Gain was 'often', not always. Transcripts were sometimes ignored by users when labelling. Stated preferences can differ from experienced ones.
agent_relevance: Here the information choice is made by prompting the LM, not by code-computed EIG; a weaker baseline.

source: Handa, Gal, Pavlick, Goodman, Andreas, Tamkin & Li (2024) Bayesian preference elicitation with language models (OPEN)
finding: OPEN uses an LM to propose features and questions but computes expected information gain with a Bayesian model over user preferences. It beat LM-only elicitation at predicting user preferences over time (TIDA metric).
numbers: Human experiment, arms of about 44 users each (for example OPEN Questions + LM Predictions: 44 users). OPEN beats naive LM prompting on time-integrated delta accuracy; open-ended questions far outperform pairwise ones. Exact TIDA values not extracted.
limits: Gain over LM-only pairwise questions was small; most benefit came from using OPEN predictions, not question choice alone. One domain (content recommendation).
agent_relevance: LM proposes, code scores with EIG. The mix beat the pure LM approach.

source: Li, Kim & Wang (2025) QuestBench: can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?
finding: On problems with exactly one missing variable, models score above 80% on math word problems but 40 to 50% or less on logic and planning problems. Ability to solve the full problem does not mean knowing which question to ask.
numbers: Models: GPT-4o, o1-preview, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro/Flash, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, Gemma 2. Logic-Q and Planning-Q under 50% accuracy; GSM-Q/GSME-Q over 80%. Best Logic-Q about 50% (49.91%, zero-shot plus CoT).
quote: models struggle to identify the right question even when they can solve the fully specified version
limits: Multiple-choice question selection with one missing variable; open-ended question writing not tested. Accuracy changes with search depth of the problem.
agent_relevance: Even frontier models without code are near coin-flip at picking the discriminating question on logic and planning. Support for computing it in code.

source: Li et al. (2025) QuestBench, prompting variants
finding: Chain-of-thought and few-shot prompting change the score only a little on the hard sets. A breadth-first-search baseline reaches high accuracy as problem depth grows.
numbers: Zero-shot, zero-shot plus CoT and four-shot rows differ by a few points on Logic-Q (roughly 25% to 39% by model). Search-depth rows: depth 3 39.0%, depth 5 80.6%, depth 10 99.8% on Logic-Q.
limits: Per-row mapping in the PDF text was garbled; rows were not fully reassigned to models.
agent_relevance: Prompt tricks give small gains; the structural fix is a search over what is unknown.

source: Ruggeri & Lombrozo (2015); Ruggeri, Lombrozo, Griffiths & Xu (2016), as cited by Mazzaccara et al. and Binz & Schulz
finding: Child studies in which EIG predicts question quality. Younger children favour hypothesis-scanning questions and shift toward constraint-seeking questions with age.
numbers: Binz & Schulz describe the Toma task, in which the right question depends on prior observations. No effect sizes read in this session.
limits: Secondhand; original papers not opened.
agent_relevance: Open these to get age curves for the human EIG benchmark.
